News.title: Married Afghan ‘killer turned his back on Christianity & acted like a single man’ before Brit found in suitcase
News.content:
THE married Afghan Christian convert accused of killing a Brit missionary reportedly turned his back on the religion before she was found dead.

Pro boxer Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, had also begun hanging around bars “as if he was a single man” in months before Elisabeth Ross’ body was found stuffed in a suitcase in central Athens.



Ahmadzai ditched his Islamic faith for Christianity after fleeing Afghanistan for Europe in 2016.

He would end up volunteering for the NGO that housed and fed him – EuroRelief – where he would meet Alaina, a wealthy and devout evangelical Christian, in 2018.



The couple tied the knot five years later and appeared to live a dream life in Athens, where they set up their own refugee charity called Love Every Nation.

But it all came crumbling down after they crossed paths with Scot aid worker Elisabeth, known as Lisa, whose body was found dumped in a derelict building on July 18.

Ahmadzai denies the killing, but admits transporting Lisa’s body in a suitcase, using her bank cards to withdraw thousands of euros, and stealing her phone to send messages that would mislead concerned loved ones.

The cracks in his marriage to Alaina had reportedly begun to show around 18 months before the shocking crime.

The American confided in two evangelical Christians from the southern US, saying she had noticed a change in her “very handsome” husband.

One of them said: “There were problems going on in the marriage.



“She felt that he had started questioning his commitment to Christianity.

“Alaina was raised in a very strong Christian home and Sharif’s childhood was obviously different coming from a strict Muslim country.

“He became more aloof and seemed more focused on boxing and his friends than doing “God’s work”, as Alaina put it.



“I think he went more to the boxing gym than to church and Alaina became worried about this.”

Alaina had also noticed that her husband was hanging around bars in Athens “as if he was a single man”.

They added: “She felt that he’d changed and wasn’t as passionate about Christianity as when they first met.”

“He converted to Christianity within a year of arriving in Greece.

“As time went on, maybe she started questioning whether he did it because he really believed in it or because he wanted to strengthen his refugee case.



“We have heard of a lot of cases like this.”

Alaina’s friends believe that Lisa, who was a devout Christian herself, got caught up in the middle of the couple’s difficulties.

One said: “Alaina is very open with her emotions. She shared this with us and I’m sure with Lisa.



“Alaina thought of Lisa as a friend and she must have confided in her.

“Maybe she challenged Sharif and he hit out in anger. He was a boxer, very strong and all it would have taken is one punch or push and somebody could get seriously injured.”

Ahmadzai had begun showing signs of disillusionment.

Facebook posts dating back to last year see him accuse some Greek NGOs of exploiting refugees and volunteers for financial gain.

He claimed that they charged volunteers registration fees and wrote of crowded accommodation and misused donations.



Ahmadzai shared images promoting the slogan “Boycott corrupt NGOs”.

The Afghan was charged homicide with intent, robbery and illegal gun possession and refused to enter a plea during a court hearing on Thursday.

Ahmadzai could now spend the next 18 months in a hellish prison with terrorists, rapists and some of Greece’s most hardened criminals.



Authorities are awaiting toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissue that will determine Elisabeth’s exact cause of death.

Alaina allegedly reported her husband to cops after she became suspicious he was involved in Elisabeth’s death.

She told cops that she had met Elisabeth through volunteer work in Athens and had last seen her on July 12, after a Bible study meeting, according to Greek news outlet Protothema.

Days later, she heard reports of a body being found stuffed in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens.

Later that night, Alaina recalled waking up with a “terrible” feeling.



In the morning she then texted Elisabeth and got two replies which made her suspicious.

Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style, both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”

When she tried calling Elisabeth she didn’t get a reply.



Alaina also told police she had grown suspicious of her husband after she woke to find him missing on the evening of July 15.

When she checked his shared location, she saw he was in Elisabeth’s flat.

Having later confronted him, he told her he had been watching a football match but had gone to Elisabeth’s apartment to use the toilet.

She told police: “I don’t know what to tell you, but all of the above made me feel strange.

“Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behaviour, I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”



Investigating officers also found CCTV footage which allegedly shows him leaving Elizabeth’s apartment with a suitcase and dropping it where her remains were discovered.

Ahmadzai has told cops he did not kill Elisabeth, saying he found her dead before panicking.

In his testimony, he reportedly said: “I never did harm to anyone. I want you to understand me and believe me. I was just in a panic.”

He is said to have claimed he had visited the house where she was staying and found her lying on the bathroom floor.

Ahmadzai claimed he panicked and fled and then encountered an elderly man near a bus stop and asked what he should do after finding a dead body.



He said he returned to the apartment the following day and placed Elisabeth’s body in a black suitcase, before placing it in the boot of the red Peugeot he drove.

“I found the old man I told you about who gave me the advice. He told me to leave the suitcase with him, and he would take care of it,” he reportedly said.

He admitted to the cops he had taken Elisabeth’s phone and bank cards.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Elisabeth’s devastated family paid tribute on Thursday – describing her as “kind, principled and selfless”.

They said: “Her integrity was absolute, and she dedicated her life to helping others in need. We are in deep pain, and we ask for time and privacy as we come to terms with our loss.”

News.title: Syrian refugee who posed as Good Samaritan to rape woman after tricking her into taxi on night out is jailed
News.content:
SINISTER ATTACK Syrian refugee who posed as Good Samaritan to rape woman after tricking her into taxi on night out is jailed

A SYRIAN refugee who posed as a “Good Samaritan” to rape a woman after tricking her into a taxi on a night out has been jailed.

Mohammed Al Masri, 25, offered to get the young mum home but instead took her back to his house where he carried out the vile sex attack, a court heard.



Al Masri and a second man followed the victim on her way home through Piccadilly Gardens, Manchester, on December 22 last year.

As she was on the phone to her boyfriend, Al Masri, who speaks Arabic and has limited English, approached the woman and pestered her with compliments.



When she became upset, he and his pal offered to get her an Uber home.

She saw them type in her address and believed them to be helping her.

But inside the cab she felt unsafe and shared her location with her boyfriend via Whatsapp, Minshull Street Crown Court heard.

The taxi driver later told police that the woman had passed out in the cab, and the two men had helped her out of the car.

She was taken into the bedroom of Al Masri’s Manchester house in Abbey Hey, where Al Masri raped her, while his friend remained in the room.

Officers arrested him soon after the attack after the young mum managed to send her live location to her boyfriend, who then alerted the police.



Cops located the address and found the woman in bed upstairs and arrested Al Masri at the scene in the early hours of December 22 last year.

Al Masri denied the offence and claimed sex was consensual, but was found guilty after a trial last month and sentenced to eight years in prison.

A 10-year sexual harm prevention order was put in place to prevent further offending.

Keith Harrison, defending Al Masri, said he was a “political refugee from the Assad regime” in Syria and that he was granted five years leave to remain, which expires in 2029.

He said Al Masri was not “work shy”, had no previous convictions, and described the offence as a “one-off”, reports the Manchester Evening News.



Judge Recorder Alexandra Simmonds said the victim was “in a vulnerable state”, “in no condition to make any free and informed decision about sexual activity”, and had to suffer the “degradation and humiliation” of the presence of a second man.

In a victim impact statement read in court, the woman said: “I will never forget the fear that I felt when this man took me to his house. I had no idea who he was.

“I had no idea where I was. I genuinely questioned if I would leave this place with my life.

“There were so many thoughts running through my mind when I arrived at his house however, this man tried to reassure me and tell me that I was going to be safe and my boyfriend was coming. This was all a sick lie.

“I remember not being able to move my body because I was so frozen with fear. I remember thinking ‘I am going to die.’



“I was thinking about my children and how they would be able to live without a mum. I just wanted it all to be over.

“The next thing I remember is the police entering the room and I have never felt relief like it. I knew I was going to live. This was not the end of what happened to me. I feel like this was only the beginning.

“I will never be able to forget what this man did to me. This man has changed me. When I met up with my friend on December 21, I was a different person then, to who I am now.”

The brave mum added: “After it all happened, I felt like I was a zombie. I could not speak to anybody. I was numb. I was emotionless. I felt nothing. I couldn’t interact with my children and felt like I was unable to be a real mum.”

Detective Constable Oliver Smith, of Greater Manchester Police, said: “I hope the sentencing of this vile sexual predator offers her a sense of solace while she looks to move on and rebuild her life.



“I urge anyone who might have experienced rape or sexual assault to please come forward and report it. You will always be listened to and supported.”

Anna Mackenzie, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “Mohammed Al Masri posed as a ‘good Samaritan’ when he offered to help the woman get a taxi home after a night out, but his motives were far more sinister.

“The way he targeted a lone woman who he believed would be vulnerable through alcohol was both calculating and insidious. Al Masri’s vile actions have had a lasting impact on the woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I truly hope today’s sentence will help her move forward, knowing that without her bravery and support this dangerous man would still be in our community.

“There is no place for rape or sexual violence in our society, and the CPS is determined to bring offenders to justice.”

News.title: Golf legend’s mansion next door to Royal Lodge on sale for £3.5million after Grand Designs-style refurbishment rejected
News.content:
IN THE ROUGH Golf legend’s mansion next door to Royal Lodge on sale for £3.5million after Grand Designs-style refurbishment rejected

GOLF legend Justin Rose’s six-bedroom mansion next door to Andrew Mountbatton-Windsor’s old Royal Lodge home, is on the market for £3.5million.

Documents seen by The Sun show the golfer, 46, and his wife Kate bought the sprawling Georgian property near the gates of the Windsor Park estate in September 2024.



The former gatehouse backs onto Windsor Great Park and forms part of the Crown Estate – near Andrew’s old home.

Rose’s links to his former neighbour, known as Randy Andy, stretch back decades to when he was an aspiring golfer.



In 1998, when Rose was one of Britain’s brightest golf prospects, Rose played a round at Sunningdale with Andrew alongside fellow young golfer Rebecca Hudson.

The future Ryder Cup star later met the then prince again when the he launched the Duke of York Champions’ Trophy, an event aimed at helping the country’s most promising juvenile golfers.

TV and radio star Chris Evans previously rented The Gate House for around two years, reportedly paying a whopping £6,000 a month.

In 2019, Evans was stopped by Andrew’s security after trying to drive through Windsor Great Park in his 1964 Aston Martin DB5.



The presenter had attempted to take a shortcut through the Crown Estate entrance in the vintage car, which is worth around £1.2million.

The route would have saved him both time and miles on a journey to a property he was renovating in Ascot, just days after Andrew stepped back from royal duties.

In April this year, just days after a heart-breaking near-miss at the Masters in Augusta, golfing icon Rose lost a planning battle over proposals to extend the Grade II-listed home in a Grand Designs-style refurbishment.

The Ryder Cup star had wanted to demolish part of the 19th-century property to build an “orangery”.

Plans also included a new ground-floor kitchen and breakfast room, bar, family area and master bedroom with a secure closet and office.



But the local council rejected the application, saying the proposed two-storey extension would be “excessively prominent, awkward, overly large” and would harm the historic building.



Rose, who is from Hampshire and has two children, appealed the decision.

But a Government planning inspector has now upheld the council’s ruling after visiting the property.

Documents show the mansion has now been put up for sale with a £3.5million asking price – £150,000 more than he bought it for.

The Rose family also own a multi-million-pound home on Surrey’s exclusive Wentworth Estate.

Andrew was forced out of Royal Lodge last year after his brother King Charles stripped him of his prince title and dukedom.



The 31-room mansion and six cottages in the estate’s grounds have since been left looking like a ghost town.

Andrew, 66, handed back his 75-year lease on Royal Lodge to the Crown Estate amid the fallout from the Jeffrey Epstein scandal last year but did not leave until February.

He has since moved into Marsh Farm on the Sandringham estate in Norfolk, with the property funded by the King.

Andrew’s peppercorn-rent deal had previously meant daughters Beatrice and Eugenie were expected to inherit the £30million mansion.

Claims Queen Camilla could inherit the property if Charles dies before her have been widely dismissed.



Prince William and Princess Kate are also not interested in moving in after securing a 20-year lease on nearby Forest Lodge.

Andrew, who was once the UK’s trade envoy, was arrested at Marsh Farm on February 19 – his birthday – by Thames Valley Police on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

Detectives then searched both his Sandringham home and his former Windsor residence, Royal Lodge.

Police have been investigating claims Andrew leaked Government information to his paedophile financier associate Jeffrey Epstein, who died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Andrew has denied any wrongdoing.



The investigation is continuing, with detectives now expected to travel to the US to speak to the family of his accuser Virginia Giuffre.

Giuffre, who took her own life last year aged 41, received a multi-million-pound payout from Andrew in an out-of-court settlement in 2022. He did not admit any liability.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Andrew was stripped of his royal titles last year.

The Sun has approached Justin Rose for comment.

News.title: Daring mission to retrieve Mount Everest ‘Green Boots’ climber after 30 years as mystery identity finally cracked
News.content:
A DANGEROUS operation is set to bring home Everest’s most infamous frozen body after the chilling mystery was finally solved after 30 years.

Known as “Green Boots” because of the distinctive lime-green footwear still protruding from the ice, the dead mountaineer has become one of the world’s most haunting landmarks.



Authorities believe the body belongs to Dorje Morup, an Indian climber who died in a savage blizzard while descending Mount Everest in 1996.

His remains have been frozen in the mountain’s deadly “death zone” ever since – more than 26,000ft above sea level.



But after three decades of mystery, a high-altitude rescue team is now being sought to attempt the perilous mission of bringing him down.

Dorje’s identity was finally established through evidence including his clothing and climbing equipment.

Authorities now hope DNA testing can provide definitive confirmation.

The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), which is funding the operation, wants his remains returned by September.

For Dorje’s family, it could finally end an agonising wait that has lasted three decades.

His wife, Konchak Yangskit, never fully accepted that her husband was dead.



She told the BBC: “On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there’d be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there.

“When he comes home, I will ask him: ‘Where were you all these years?’”

Dorje had left home in Ladakh in 1996 with a heroic promise.

He told his wife he would return from Everest as a hero and make his country proud.



Konchak told the BBC: “He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return.

“I wondered if I was ever going to see him again.”

Dorje was a 48-year-old lance naik, or lance corporal, in the ITBP and an experienced Himalayan trekker.

He was one of six climbers attempting to make history by reaching Everest’s summit from the treacherous Chinese side.



Three members of the expedition turned back when a savage snowstorm swept across the mountain.

Dorje continued towards the 8,849m summit with fellow climbers Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor.

The trio eventually radioed their team leader at around 3.45pm Nepal time, reporting that they had reached the summit.

Poor visibility may have made it impossible to establish exactly where they were.

Howling winds ripped across Everest, temperatures plunged and visibility collapsed.



From below, members of the expedition spotted two headlamps moving above the Second Step at around 28,000ft.

It was the last time the three men were seen alive.

Dorje’s body lies in Everest’s notorious “death zone”, where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are around a third of those at sea level.

The Tibetan side of the mountain is particularly treacherous, with steeper terrain and fewer rescue facilities than the southern route.

The ITBP is now looking for a specialist mountain rescue group capable of taking on the dangerous mission.



If successful, his remains will be taken back to India for DNA testing – and if the tests confirm his identity, his family will finally be able to bury him.

“The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial,” said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions.

“The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side,” he told BBC Hindi.

Sherpa sources told BBC News Nepali that the lack of support on the Chinese side makes the recovery even more daunting.

Mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said bringing the body down would be brutally difficult even in the more favourable spring season.



“It’s really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That’s the simple reason it is still there for so many years,” he said.

“There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point.”

The frozen remains would then have to be physically hauled down the mountain to an altitude where they could be collected by helicopter or possibly transported by yaks.

Bodies trapped in iced-up climbing gear can weigh several times the average man and become brutally difficult to move across Everest’s unforgiving terrain.

The remains can also begin to defrost and decompose once they reach lower altitudes.



Indian climber Kuntal Joisher warned the first stage of the descent could be the most dangerous of all.

“It’s going to be very, very risky endeavour. It’s extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge.

“The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body.”

Experts say even relatively straightforward recoveries can cost between $40,000 and $80,000.

Recovering bodies from Everest has become more common over the past decade, but many of the hundreds who have died on the mountain remain where they fell.



Testimony from surviving members of the expedition, the location of the climbers’ final radio contact and Dorje’s clothing and equipment eventually led authorities to his identity.

An ITBP official, speaking anonymously, told BBC News Hindi that new evidence helped identify Dorje in recent years.

“We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time,” the official said.

For years, the family had only medals, trophies and a handful of photographs from Dorje’s mountain adventures to remember him by.

They also kept a certificate from the Chinese government stating that at 17:30 on May 10, 1996, Dorje reached the summit of Everest.



His son Punchok Dorjai says that if his father is finally brought home, the family will hold a funeral near Martyrs Park in Ladakh’s capital Leh.

“My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr,” Dorje said.

He said Dorje’s teammates who died alongside him deserve the same honour.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And the family already knows what they will do with one extraordinary reminder of the man who became an Everest mystery.

“We are planning to keep the Green Boots.”

News.title: Detective sacked for calling trans women ‘c**ks in frocks’ blasts decision insisting she’s ‘protecting female rights’
News.content:
A POLICE officer who was sacked after she opposed a policy which could have required her to strip search biological males says she has become a ‘scapegoat’ for speaking out about women’s rights.

Rachel Fletcher, a former detective constable, was horrified by new guidance which enabled officers and some detainees to self identify as men or women.



The framework meant that female officers could be required to conduct intimate searches of trans women who didn’t have a gender recognition certificate and hadn’t undergone reassignment surgery.

It also enabled biological male officers, identifying as women, to remove the clothing of female detainees when looking for forbidden objects.



The National Police Chief’s Council (NPCC) guidance, in place between 2022 and early 2024, was later suspended after criticism from politicians and amid legal concerns.

But last week Fletcher, who says she was an outspoken advocate for women’s rights and openly challenged the strip search policy, was hauled before a panel at Houghton Police Station near Sunderland.



The former detective, who worked in Northumbria Police’s Child Protection team, was told comments she had made about men and trans women amounted to “hatred”, and her behaviour was ruled gross misconduct.

Fletcher was accused of using the phrase “c***s in frocks” while discussing the controversial strip search policy with colleagues, an allegation she denies.



It was also claimed that Fletcher, who worked on an array of harrowing abuse cases, commented “all men are rapists” and “no wonder a f***ing man did it”, while talking about a crime.

Speaking after her sacking, the 49-year-old said: “I have been made a scapegoat.

“This isn’t about throwaway comments I might or might not have made.

“This has happened because I dared to speak out about the rights of women and girls.

“The strip search policy at the time was unlawful, and I dared to have an opinion on it. That’s my only crime.



“It was the most egregious, anti-dignity and unlawful guidance you could come up with and I don’t know how it got through.

“It was dangerous and irresponsible.

“No female officer should ever be in that position.”



After the Supreme Court’s ruling in April 2025, the NPCC issued new interim guidance making biological sex the default for intimate and strip searches.

The earlier policy enabling officers and some detainees to self identify was developed under the NPCC’s LGBTQ+ portfolio, led by Vanessa Jardine, the current chief constable of Northumbria Police.

It read: “Chief Officers are advised to recognise the status of Transgender colleagues from the moment they transition, considered to be, the point at which they present in the gender with which they identify.”

It added: “Thus, once a Transgender colleague has transitioned, they will search persons of the same gender as their own lived gender.”

In relation to detainees it reads: “All searches are dealt with on a case by case basis after consideration by a custody sergeant based on the response of the detainee.”



The guidance became highly controversial as it changed the policy of same sex searches to those based on gender identity.

In February 2024, it was criticised by the then Policing Minister Chris Philp who said: “It is not right, safe or respectful to detainees of either sex for officers to conduct searches on the basis of gender self-identification.”

Fletcher was a highly respected officer who recently led the investigation into the crimes of 39-year-old paedophile Ross Jackson.

He was later found guilty of 24 separate sexual offences and was jailed for 23 years at Newcastle Crown Court in February.

After she was sacked, Rachel’s supporters set up a GoFundMe page, which has so far raised £21,549 to help her and her children while she finds a new job.



She said: “If you’re in the police you’re not allowed to talk about misogyny or to call out gender ideology.

“I’ve been shut down for standing up for women’s rights.

“One of the comments I made was something along the lines of, imagine you are a female student officer and you are asked to carry out a strip search of a person you’ve been told is a woman, only to find they have a co**.

“How would she feel? Would she have the confidence to object?

“The crude language I used is commonplace in the office I worked in, where we spent every day describing the mechanics of sexual offences.



“It’s really difficult and horrible to be in this position but it’s the only way we are going to change things.

“If cops aren’t willing to stand up and sacrifice to do the right thing then who will?”

Fletcher was told she was being referred to the Professional Standards Department (PSD) on January 9 2024 after allegedly making the comments between February and December 2023.

She was put on limited duties after that, which meant she had no contact with the public.

On February 14 of the same year she was served with papers, informing her case would be going before a panel, chaired by Assistant Chief Constable Andy Hill.



Then, last week, it was ruled comments she was alleged to have made amounted to gross misconduct and she was sacked.

It was found Fletcher had breached the Standards of Professional Behaviour in relation to discreditable conduct, authority, respect and courtesy and equality and diversity.

She added: “I am absolutely devastated to have lost the job I loved.

“My dream was always to be a detective.

“At times my work was harrowing and really emotionally exhausting, but so rewarding.



“It was a real privilege.

“Policing is still very male dominated and it always has been.

“I think my sacking will have a negative impact on my colleagues. They will be terrified to speak up or challenge anything in case they are also dismissed.

“If I could have my job back, I would in a heartbeat because it’s such important work, I loved it.

“I don’t know what I’m going to do next – but I’ll keep going.



“It’s lovely to have this support and just incredible.

“People who have donated have given me peace of mind that I don’t have to worry about paying the mortgage or feeding my kids.”

During the hearing she admitted she said, “the only way to stop night time rapes is to put a 9 o’clock curfew on all men”, or words to that effect.

However, the former detective, who had worked at the force for 23-years, insists she was joking.

But the panel ruled Fletcher had made all the comments and dismissed her.



A spokesperson for Northumbria Police said: “The allegations faced were as follows:

“Between February and December 2023 and whilst on duty, the officer made comments about or in relation to men in general that were sexist, inappropriate and offensive.

“In or around January 2024, whilst on duty, the officer made a comment about transgender women in general which was transphobic, inappropriate and/or offensive.

“The panel found gross misconduct was proven in relation to both allegations and the officer was dismissed without notice.”

The National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) was also contacted for comment.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

It emphasised that new guidance was issued last May which makes clear police searches “such as those which expose intimate body parts, should be carried out by police officers and staff of the same biological sex as the detained person”.

However, it adds that “there may be very limited exceptions considered where someone requests to be searched by an officer of their gender”.

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ in broad daylight attack at country park – as cops hunt man in his 30s
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

PARK HORROR Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ in broad daylight attack at country park – as cops hunt man in his 30s

A WOMAN was allegedly sexually assaulted at a park in a sickening broad daylight attack.

Cops said they have stepped up patrols in the area as detectives hunt a man described as white and aged in his 30s.

The sexual assault reportedly happened in a wooded area of Newstead and Annesley Country Park in Nottinghamshire.

The force said the incident occurred shortly after 11am on Tuesday (August 4).





Officers have launched a major investigation and increased their presence in the area.

Detective Inspector Ed Cook, of Nottinghamshire Police, has sought to reassure the community.

He said: “While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, they are obviously very concerning for the public.

“I would like to reassure people we have a large team of officers working on this investigation and we are doing everything we can to find the person responsible.

“The suspect has been described as a white man aged in his 30s.

“Public safety remains our top priority and extra patrols will continue to be carried out in the area.

“I’d also encourage the public to remain vigilant and report any suspicious or concerning behaviour to us immediately.”

Police have urged anyone who saw anything suspicious around the time of the attack to come forward.



Officers are also appealing for anyone with information which could help identify the suspect to contact them.

Anyone with information is asked to call Nottinghamshire Police on 101, quoting incident number 38 of 7 August.

Information can also be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Terrifying moment huge hippo charges at boat full of tourists as beast lunges out of the water in pursuit
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a huge hippo charges at a boat packed with tourists before lunging through the water in a furious pursuit.

Viral footage captures the heart-stopping moment the massive male beast suddenly gives chase in Botswana, forcing the fleeing boat to speed away.



The tourists had been hoping for a glimpse of Africa’s spectacular wildlife when they spotted the lone hippo in the distance.

But their thrilling wildlife encounter quickly turned into a terrifying battle to escape the enormous beast.



The captain slowed the boat to avoid disturbing the territorial animal before issuing a chilling warning to his passengers.

Oznur Bell, the tourist who captured the moment on camera said: “After watching his behaviour for a moment, he calmly said, ‘Hold on-we need to speed up now before he decides to come after us.’



“The moment we accelerated, we looked back and realized the hippo was chasing us.”

The shocking footage shows the hulking animal powering through the water as it relentlessly pursues the boat.

For several terrifying moments, the tourists were left staring back at the furious beast as it bobbed in and out of the water behind them.

The videographer said: “For a few moments, every single person in the boat was genuinely worried.”



Oznur described the terrifying encounter as “one of the most terrifying moments I’ve ever experienced.”

According to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, common hippos can grow to a staggering 16.5ft long and 5.2ft tall at the shoulder.

Adult males can weigh between 3,500 and almost 10,000lbs – making the colossal mammals roughly the weight of a mid-length SUV.

Despite their fearsome size and reputation, hippos are herbivores and do not view humans as prey.

Researchers at the University of Pretoria say hippos kill around 500 people across Africa every year – more than twice as many as lions.



The enormous animals are territorial and can aggressively defend their patches of water.

That means an unsuspecting boat entering their territory can quickly become a dangerous target.

The monstrous male eventually called off the chase, allowing the shaken tourists to escape.

But the dramatic encounter also showcased the astonishing way hippos move through shallow water.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Rather than relying solely on traditional swimming strokes, the powerful animals can propel themselves by pushing off the bottom in a bizarre galloping or bounding motion.



The furious hippo put the remarkable technique on full display as it thundered through the water after the fleeing boat.

News.title: Are twisted Russian civilians PAYING drone pilots to carry out sick ‘human safari’ attacks on innocent Ukrainians?
News.content:
TWISTED Russian civilians have been accused of paying for sick “human safari” hunting missions targeting defenceless Ukrainians on the streets.

Drone pilots working within the Russian army are “wilfully targeting civilians for monetary gain” under Vladimir Putin‘s evil rule, a former Nato analyst told The Sun.



Terrifying footage this week showed Yuriy, a 52-year-old grocer, running for his life as he was chased down by a Kremlin suicide drone.

The Ukrainian was left with serious shrapnel wounds as the UAV exploded as it struck the grocer’s tent where he was selling fruit and vegetables.



Harrowing footage was released just a few days later and captured another drone attack on a Ukrainian civilian in Sumy.

A Russian drone pursues a local appearing to toy with him before the operator makes the drone explode in a huge blast.

The horror scenes make up just a couple of the thousands of senseless attacks on civilians by Russia during the war in Ukraine with Kherson becoming known as the grim epicentre of the attacks.

Dr Patrick Bury, a warfare and counter-terrorism expert and former Nato analyst, says the brutality highlights how Putin has created a regime which is “completely rotten to the core”.



He told The Sun: “[Russia is] going in and they’re basically intentionally targeting civilians.

“It’s become known as the Kherson safari, essentially civilian hunting missions.

“It shows we’re at the real bottom of the barrel of human conduct in war.”

Dr Bury says the human safaris would be considered one of the worst atrocities committed by Moscow should they ever face consequences.

The term human safari is most well known due to the 1990s siege of Sarajevo.



Wealthy tourists were accused of making weekend trips to the besieged city and paying Serbian fighters to shoot civilians in the streets.

Dr Bury fears a similar pattern of abuse could be repeated in Ukraine after several worrying reports from independent journalists in Kyiv.

He claims: “It looks like a fusion between military units like the eighth Artillery Regiment and certain people in there who are drone operators.



“They have been accused of using crowdfunding from Russian civilians to gain money.

“They’re wilfully targeting civilians for monetary gain and propaganda gain.

“The fact that there’s been no one brought to task speaks volumes about the Russian military – the laws of war are clearly not a priority for them.”

In Kherson alone, Human Rights Watch (HRW) found at least 45 drone strikes carried out by Russian forces that appeared to deliberately target civilians.

Dozens of these cases were filmed and shared across Russian social media and Telegram channels.



In almost every example seen, HRW claims they believe the drone operator was purposely targeting a civilian or civilian infrastructure like a bus or parking lot.

Intentionally killing civilians during an armed conflict is a serious war crime, under international humanitarian law, such as the Geneva Conventions.

A United Nations probe during the conflict has found Russia guilty of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied regions of Ukraine.



The UN report states that large numbers of Ukrainian civilians have been targeted in a “widespread and systematic manner” at the hands of Russia.

Ukraine’s former deputy minister at the Ministry of Internal Affairs Anton Gerashchenko also condemned the human hunts.

He blasted: “Russian human safari is spreading. Russia‘s war crimes are mounting up.”

Back in April, three separate strikes on public spaces in the Nikopol district killed 10 and injured over 50 civilians within three days.

Russian FPVs hit two passenger buses, killing four civilians while a second in the nearby Chervonohryhorivka municipality wounded five.



A drone also struck a civilian car, killing one and injuring another as a day earlier five were killed when a Kremlin drone struck a civilian market in Nikopol.

Much like this year, the number of civilian attacks often surges in summer, Dr Bury says.

“Between summer 2025 and by October 2025, it was up to about 200 confirmed dead and over 2,000 wounded in these kinds of attacks.

“And they’re targeting everyone, they’re targeting shops, people going out for a cigarette, children in playgrounds even people on their way home from work.”

One of the scariest parts of these attacks is how defenceless the civilians are when the deadly UAVs lock onto their positions.



The drones can be operated by a soldier who watches a camera which allows them to track a target even if they try to run or hide.

“It’s not as if civilians in these areas are equipped with electromagnetic jammers so you can hear them and take cover and that is about it,” Dr Bury added.

For experts such as Patrick, the fact Russians allegedly partake in such heinous activities comes down to the example set by their despotic leader.

Dr Bury said: “There’s a lot of great things that have come out of Russia but ultimately it is quite a brutalised place, especially since the Soviets.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“And certainly in this war, you get to the front line and you’re put into a meat storm where you’re given a gun and then just told to charge the enemy to be quickly wiped down in a human wave attack.



“I think all this plays into a kind of normalisation of this kind of brutal behaviour.”

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' when he was general secretary
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy
News.content:
Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC's Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.

Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me."

"It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added.

"It's not fairâ¦ All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution - or his father's legacy.

He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration.

"I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

"There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.

President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".

The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024.

News.title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
News.content:
Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner Kevin Southworth has acknowledged that failures to remand Levy in custody during court hearings in May and June 2025 left him free to commit further offences.

BTP confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.

Crime and policing minister Sarah Jones said the situation "raises serious questions".

"The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning."

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect.

"In particular, there were points where we could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail, based on the information available."

Victims' Commissioner for London Andrea Simons called for a "multi-agency review" over the "litany of failures to manage such a prolific offender".

She told BBC Breakfast that public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".

She continued: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."

Lisa Squire, whose daughter Libby was murdered by a man who had previously committed a string of sex crimes, told the BBC that a "catalogue of disasters" had led to Levy's murders.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme "the patterns were there, he was flying those red flags", and said there were "precursor offences" for which he could have stopped by police.

"At the moment, the message going out, in my opinion, is that women's safety is not important," she continued.

ZoÃ« Billingham, a former independent police inspector who pushed for reforms on how violence against women in girls is policed, said that "too often in cases like this the dots aren't being joined up".

She added: "It's not one or two missed opportunities that could have brought him to justice, that could have had him locked up and behind bars and no longer a threat to women and girls. It was an extraordinary succession."

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: Police failings revealed as sex offender left free to murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was all right, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent BTP investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple's manager Vickie White confirmed the split, which was first reported by the Sun newspaper, external.

She said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago.

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: How asylum protests brought disorder to Thetford
News.content:
It is normally a quiet residential street but on Wednesday night, Clover Way erupted.

Residents later described their shock at seeing hundreds of people converging on an address where they believed asylum seekers were being housed.

It was one of five locations across the Norfolk town of Thetford that saw sporadic violence and disorder over three consecutive evenings, beginning on Tuesday.

Two police officers were taken to hospital, including one who had been bitten, and there were arrests on suspicion of offences including public order, harassment and possession of an offensive weapon.

Andy Symonds, the chair of the Norfolk Police Federation, said Friday night had been "much calmer", although "a number of people" had been dispersed using powers from Section 35 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014.

"We are on watch for tonight, it's the weekend. We will be dispersing people from the area," he told the BBC.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: How mum joined ‘rising number of hidden homeless’ after fleeing with daughter
News.content:
When Jodie and her daughter had to flee their hometown, they could only take what they could carry - two black bin bags filled with their belongings.

Jodie, then aged 30, found herself in Margate, Kent, with a seven-year-old child to take care of and no place to live.

"I had to leave everything," Jodie said. "The bags were mainly my daughter's clothes and her dolls."

Having left after feeling threatened, she chose the seaside town where they had been on summer and half term holidays, although it meant leaving her family and friends behind.

"I wanted to go somewhere that wasn't very alien for my daughter," said Jodie, now 42.

"It was still scary, but I had to be the strong one and protect her. I had to do it so that my daughter could have a life."

After a brief stay in council emergency accommodation, she said they spent a year sleeping on the sofas and floors of people she had met in Margate.

News.title: Pokémon hobby takes brothers to world championships
News.content:
What began as a hobby for two brothers from Nottinghamshire is taking them to the US as they prepare to compete at the PokÃ©mon World Championships.

Thirteen-year-old Oliver, who became a European champion aged 12, will compete alongside his brother Edward, 11, who will play in the junior division.

The pair, from Ruddington, first started playing the trading card game at a Nottingham board game cafe when their mum wanted to get them out of the house and away from screens after the Covid-19 pandemic.

Oliver and Edward will join thousands of competitors at this year's world championships in San Francisco, taking place between 28 and 30 August.

Mum Kayleigh said: "It's crazy, I never thought that PokÃ©mon would take me around the world and the kids.

"It's a lovely community, the kids love competing, it's such a nice atmosphere."

Police have launched a renewed appeal for information regarding a Birmingham woman who vanished almost 50 years ago.

Sarjit Kaur Mann was just 20 years old when she was last seen in September 1976, following a family holiday in France.

Officers issued the fresh plea on Saturday, which would have marked her 70th birthday, hoping to shed new light on her disappearance.

Originally from Birmingham and a student at the University of Birmingham, Sarjit had been on holiday with her family in Antibes, southern France.

She asked to remain behind when her family returned home, expressing a desire to spend more time with people she had met and explore local museums.

Her family subsequently travelled back to Britain, but Sarjit was never seen again.

open image in gallery Antibes is located between Cannes and Nice on the South Eastern coast of France ( Google Maps )

Police have revealed that a woman named Jane, whom Sarjit reportedly met, is said to have telephoned the family a few days after their return, claiming that Sarjit had drowned.

However, she gave no further information and abruptly ended the call.

“What happened to Sarjit in France remains a mystery and we have always kept an open mind,” Pc Shaun Reeve, from the West Midlands Police missing person investigation unit, said.

“At the time, Sarjit was said to have met a group of young women of a similar age, one of whom was called Jane.

“We believe Jane called Sarjit’s family a few days after they returned home and told them their daughter had drowned before hanging up.

“Whether this caller was Jane or not, we do not know. The caller was never identified and Sarjit has never been found.

“What we are hoping for is that someone who knew Sarjit and her family at the time might be able to help us piece together more about her life around the time she went missing.

“Even though this was a long time ago, we will never stop investigating any new information we receive as we try to bring some answers, or closure, to Sarjit’s family after nearly 50 years.”

Anyone who thinks they can help with the investigation is asked to phone the team directly on 0121 626 7003.

The Met Office has revealed the best locations to view the UK’s fullest solar eclipse for the next 54 years on Wednesday – with Devon and Cornwall the top destinations for the event.

More than 90% of the sun will be obscured by the moon between 6.17pm and 8.06pm on August 12, the most it has been blocked above UK skies since the total eclipse in 1999.

Devon, Cornwall and the westernmost parts of Pembrokeshire in Wales are set to see the eclipse at its fullest, with a range of 94% to 96% of the sun obscured by the moon.

Plymouth in particular is forecast to see the moon cover 94.66% of the sun at 7.16pm on Wednesday, according to the Met Office.

The rest of Wales, Northern Ireland, parts of the West Midlands and the South West, and the westernmost parts of Scotland can expect to see 92% to 94% solar coverage.

In Cardiff, the moon is forecast to obscure 93.24% of the sun at 7.13pm while in Belfast it will cover 93.09% of the sun at 7.08pm.

Skygazers in the rest of the UK will likely see the moon obscure 90% to 92% of the sun – with 91.79% expected in Birmingham at 7.12pm, 91.41% in London at 7.13pm, 90.74% in Inverness at 7.03pm, 90.71% in Edinburgh at 7.06pm and 90.22% in Newcastle at 7.07pm.

Those most keen to catch a sight of the fullest possible solar eclipse should avoid the easternmost parts of the UK, where only 88% to 90% of solar coverage is expected.

These include the coasts of Norfolk, Yorkshire and Aberdeenshire, as well as the Orkney and Shetland Islands.

The Royal Greenwich Observatory also warned the public that regular sunglasses are not a safe enough method to view the cosmic phenomenon.

Imo Bell, a planetarium astronomer at the observatory, previously told the Press Association: “It’s not a total eclipse, but over 90% is really exciting. We’re not going to get one this good for a really long time.

“So, it’s important not to miss it, and to be prepared. You can’t just go out and expect to have a look because it’s really dangerous for your eyes.

“So, you can use solar eclipse glasses, which are very, very different from sunglasses – they block out so much light that you can’t see anything through them except the sun, because that’s how much light they need to block for the damaging light of the sun to be safe to view.

“Ideally a solar telescope is an amazing way to witness it, and if you don’t have one of them then you can look into whether your local astronomy society is doing any events.

“And if all else fails, you can project the image of the eclipse using a household item like a colander which has lots of holes in – point the colander towards the Sun with your back facing it, and in the shadow of the colander you’ll be able to see the eclipse in the holes, which is really cool.”

The next time the moon obscures as much of the sun will be in 2081 and the next total solar eclipse in the UK will be in 2090.

Ms Bell advised getting to a vantage point facing west, with minimal buildings around, as the best way to view the eclipse.

“We might notice the sky getting a little bit dark, so if you’re looking safely, it’ll look a bit like the moon is taking a bite out of the sun, you’ll see something that looks a bit like a crescent sun.”

Reykjavik in Iceland and Spanish cities A Coruna, Oviedo, Zaragoza, Bilbao and Valencia will see a total eclipse on Wednesday, in which the moon fully obscures the sun.
