World.title: Document reveals EFCC secured court order to freeze two more Osun govt accounts
World.content:
Fuller details about the recent account freeze launched against the Osun State Government by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) have emerged, bringing to light a wider extent of an action that has already dealt a severe blow to the agency’s reputation.

Sahara Reporters has freshly reported that the EFCC targeted not just one of the state government’s accounts as previously known, but three.

These include one federal allocation account with First Bank, which was previously known to be the only state government account the EFCC had frozen. The other two, just revealed, are joint allocation accounts with Zenith Bank.

Sahara Reporters reported that the commission indeed obtained a court order to implement the account freeze as disclosed for the first time on Thursday by President Bola Tinubu.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The freeze order has drawn widespread condemnation to the EFCC and its chairman, Ola Olukoyede, as a politically motivated step.

The action came just over a week before the 15 August governorship election in Osun State, where incumbent Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party is running against Bola Oyebamiji belonging to the president’s party, the All Progressives Congress (APC).

It fed into a broader perception that federal agencies, including the Nigerian police, have been bias and selective in its enforcement actions against the Accord Party and Governor Adeleke’s second term bid in the forthcoming election.

Expressing deep embarrassment about the development on Thursday, Mr Tinubu ordered the EFCC in a statement he signed personally to immediately take steps to vacate the court order freezing the state government’s account.

Documents newly obtained by Sahara Reporters showed that the EFCC obtained a freeze order against three accounts of the state government from the Federal High Court in Abuja on 5 August (Wednesday) through an ex parte application instituted under suit number FHC/ABJ/CS/1750/2026.

The application being ex parte meant that the adverse party that would be affected by the order sought was not meant to participate in its hearing.

According to Sahara Reporters, EFCC’s lawyer, M. A. Babatunde, moved the motion ex parte, informing the court that the affected accounts were “currently being investigated in a case of Diversion of public funds and Money Laundering pending conclusion of investigation and prosecution.”

The ex parte application was supported by an affidavit sworn by EFC’s investigator Ikenna Chukwueze and an exhibit marked “EFCC 1.”

The three frozen accounts

After listening to the lawyer, Justice Mohammed Umar went on to issue the ex parte order authorising the EFCC chairman, Ola Olukoyede, “or any officer authorised by him,” to direct the managing directors of the affected banks to freeze accounts listed in the schedule to the application.

The schedule listed three accounts of the Osun State Government affected by the court order. They are:

Osun State Government Federal Allocation Account, domiciled with First Bank Plc, Account No. 2017170947;

Osun State Joint Allocation Account, domiciled with Zenith Bank Plc, Account No. 1013374191; and

Osun State Joint Allocation Account, domiciled with Zenith Bank Plc, Account No. 1014374909.

Justice Umar ordered that the freeze on the accounts should be in place till the conclusion of EFCC’s investigations.

Until Sahara Reporters’ reporting, only the First Bank account was known to be affected by the freeze order.

It is not clear yet why the anti-corruption agency has concealed the full information from the public in its communications on the matter since Wednesday when the EFCC wrote to First Bank to impose a Post-No-Debit (PND) restriction on an account operated by the Osun State Government.

The letter dated 5 July (Wednesday) did not cite any court order and only referenced just one account of the state government.

A statement from the EFCC that same day gave the impression that only one account was targeted and confirmed the restriction on the account through a PND directive to the bank.

Also, EFCC’s Director of Public Affairs, Wilson Uwujaren, appeared on Arise Television earlier on Thursday to justify the freeze of the state government’s account without a court order. However, Mr Uwujaren disclosed during the interview that the commission would follow up with a court order within 72 hours of the PND restriction, citing the EFCC’s establishment law.

The first indication of a court’s involvement in the account freeze came on Thursday from President Tinubu’s statement directing the EFCC to immediately take steps to vacate the freeze order.

Mr Tinubu, echoing public outrage about the EFCC’s action coming about 10 days before the 15 August Osun State governorship election, said he was deeply embarrassed by the freeze order.

It is not clear yet if the EFCC has applied to the court to lift the freeze orders.

‘Embarrassment’ to the president

PREMIUM TIMES reported on Wednesday that the EFCC froze an account of the Osun State Government domiciled with First Bank, after which the anti-graft agency said the action followed suspicious movement of public funds from the account amid an ongoing investigation into alleged financial misconduct involving about 11N billion in Ecology Funds, Intervention Funds and Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) allocations.

On Thursday, Mr Tinubu directed the EFCC to lift the restriction on the account, describing the timing of the action, coming about 10 days before the governorship election, as inauspicious and capable of creating the impression that a federal agency was being used to interfere with the poll.

The president said he found the EFCC’s action deeply embarrassing.

“I must state that I feel deeply embarrassed not by the EFCC’s exercise of its mandate backed by a court order, but by the timing of the agency’s action,” Mr Tinubu wrote.

“This is so because every action taken by an institution of State, especially at the Federal level, is always credited to me, as the President, even when I may not have had any prior knowledge of the action.”

He said while he intentionally refrained from directing or interfering in the operational activities of the EFCC or any other investigative or prosecutorial agency, he felt compelled to intervene in the Osun State matter.

“Osun State is only a few days away from its gubernatorial election. Therefore, nothing ought to be done to give an impression that the EFCC or indeed any other agency of the federal government is being used to interfere with the election.

“Based on the foregoing premise, I am duty-bound to issue a directive on this issue in consonance with the overriding public interest in preserving public confidence and the integrity, credibility, and fairness of our democratic process,” Mr Tinubu stated.

“Accordingly, I have directed the EFCC to immediately proceed to the court to vacate the order and discontinue whatever action it has instituted against the Osun State Government in this regard.”

The directive marks a dramatic intervention by the president in a controversy that has dominated political discourse in Osun State over the past 24 hours, after the anti-graft agency froze one of the state’s accounts over an ongoing investigation into the alleged diversion of about N11 billion in public funds.

Presidential spokesman, Mr Onanuga subsequently announced on Thursday that Mr Tinubu spoke with Mr Adeleke in a phone conversation, informing the governor that he had directed to lift the order restricting the account of the Osun State Government.

World.title: Turaki-led PDP meets UK High Commission, raises concerns over alleged Nigeria’s shrinking opposition space
World.content:
The Kabiru Turaki-led faction of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has raised m concerns over what it described as mounting threats to Nigeria’s multi-party democracy.

The faction raised the concerns during a meeting with officials of the United Kingdom High Commission, where it accused the federal government of weakening democratic institutions and stifling opposition politics.

The meeting, held between the UK High Commission delegation and the PDP’s interim leadership led by former Minister of Special Duties Kabiru Turaki (SAN), focused on the state of Nigeria’s democracy, the role of the opposition and the country’s political outlook ahead of the 2026 and 2027 electoral cycles.

According to a statement issued on Thursday by the PDP Interim National Working Committee through its National Publicity Secretary, Ini Ememobong, the discussions formed part of the party’s ongoing engagement with members of the international community on developments in Nigeria’s political space.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The UK delegation was led by Fortune Aldred, Senior Political Adviser at the British High Commission, alongside Stephen Asek, Political Adviser (Cameroon).

Other members of the PDP team at the meeting included the National Secretary, Wonyengikuro Daniel, National Treasurer, Isa Abubakar, National Organising Secretary Theophilus Shan, National Legal Adviser Shafi Bara’u, Principal Private Secretary to the Chairman Ibrahim Abdullahi and Mr Ememobong.

PDP alleges shrinking democratic space

The opposition party said discussions centred on what it called the “asphyxiation of the opposition,” the prolonged leadership crisis within the PDP, the political outlook ahead of future elections and issues surrounding former President Goodluck Jonathan’s possible candidature in the 2027 presidential election.

Although the statement did not disclose the position taken on Mr Jonathan’s possible return to electoral politics, it identified the issue as one of the major subjects discussed during the engagement.

Mr Turaki told the UK delegation that preserving a vibrant opposition remained essential for the survival of Nigeria’s democracy.

“The need to ensure the survival of multi-party democracy and the opposition remains critical to a thriving democratic system,” the factional chairman was quoted as saying.

He further accused the All Progressives Congress (APC)-led federal administration of pursuing what he described as a “state capture disposition,” alleging that the government was systematically attempting to dominate the political landscape.

According to him, the actions of the federal government had heightened political tensions across the country.

“The political temperature of the country has risen to fever-pitch levels, traceable majorly to the actions and inactions of the APC-led federal government, who are relentlessly provocative in their desire to forcefully capture every part of our country,” he said.

The PDP also linked its engagement with the British diplomats to recent political developments, including President Bola Tinubu’s widely reported remark that “all is fair in politics,” which the party alleged had encouraged the weaponisation of state institutions against opposition parties.

UK High Commission responds

Responding on behalf of the British delegation, Mr Aldred thanked the PDP factional leadership for the engagement and assured the party that the issues raised would be communicated through the High Commission’s established diplomatic reporting channels.

He, however, stressed that Nigeria remained a sovereign nation whose political affairs were for Nigerians to determine.

According to the statement, Mr Aldred said the responsibility of the High Commission was to understand political developments in Nigeria and relay its observations through appropriate diplomatic mechanisms.

The Kabiru Turaki-led PDP faction is one of the rival camps laying claim to the leadership of Nigeria’s main opposition party.

The faction operates with an Interim National Working Committee headed by Mr Turaki, with Mr Ememobong serving as its spokesperson, amid an ongoing leadership dispute with a rival camp over control of the party.

The other faction is led by Abdulrahman Mohammed and backed by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, a PDP member serving in the APC-led federal government.

The Mohammed-led was recognised by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), which recently gave it access to its portal to upload its candidates for the 2027 general election.

It is unclear whether the High Commission has met with the group.

World.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, Pakistan sign joint defence agreement
World.content:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye on Friday signed a joint defence agreement to deepen security cooperation amid heightened military tensions and conflicts in the Middle East.

The agreement, identified as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, was initiated to strengthen deterrence against attacks on any of the signatories.

It stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, they said in a joint statement.

According to a joint statement by Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Saudi state media on Friday, the agreement was signed by the three Sunni Muslim-majority states in Mecca, the holiest site in Islam.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

“The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.

“It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three States,” the statement read.

The Middle East war between the US and Iran significantly impacted Gulf states, which have been the primary targets of Iranian retaliatory strikes since the war began in February. PREMIUM TIMES reported attacks on Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure and oil facilities earlier in the year.

A new front of the war opened in July between Riyadh and Yemen’s rebel group, the Houthis. This paper reported that Saudi Arabia’s national oil company shut down its Jazan oil refinery after a Houthi missile attack damaged key facilities last week. In response to the months-long war that continues to threaten its economy, Saudi Arabia has been seeking to diversify its defence partnerships.

Although Turkiye and Pakistan have not been subjected to direct attacks, both are eager to calm regional conflicts that threaten their security and economies.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, explained that the pact is not a threat to any country in the region.

It also stated that it was “not linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race, but rather to building sustainable, self-reliant capabilities.”

According to Pakistan’s Sharif, the joint pact serves “the interests of our homelands and enhances the security and stability of our region.”

However, Iranian lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei warned that it would take more than the pact to achieve regional security.

“Saudis must know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided nursing to the Americans did not bring them security,” he wrote on X.

World.title: Gov Lawal receives ZIK Pan-African Leadership Award in Ghana
World.content:
Zamfara State Governor, Dauda Lawal has been honoured with the ZIK International Peace and Leadership Award in Ghana, recognising his administration’s notable achievements over the past three years.

The 7th ZIK International Peace and Leadership Award ceremony was held on Friday at the British Council in Accra, Ghana.

This year’s theme for the lecture was “Leadership, Peace, and Regional Integration: Advancing Africa’s Development in a Changing Global Order.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The award’s board and governing council emphasised, among other reasons for the honour, Governor Lawal’s significant progress in public sector leadership and economic reforms in Zamfara State.

The Board of Trustees (BOT) chairman of the ZIK Pan-African Award, His Royal Highness Professor Echefuna R G Onyeabadi, stated that the award aims to recognise individuals making meaningful contributions in service to the people.

In his remarks after receiving the award, Governor Lawal expressed his gratitude and commitment to doing more to help rescue and rebuild Zamfara State.

He said: “This award is dedicated to all the people of Zamfara State. My administration has been working tirelessly to ensure the state can compete with any other in Nigeria. That was our promise, and we have surpassed expectations in just three years.

“My administration has transformed Zamfara through urban renewal initiatives; we constructed a modern, state-of-the-art airport, something that had not existed for over 30 years since the state’s founding.

“We have made great strides in security, civil service reform, education, health, and other sectors.

“I appreciate the organisers of this annual lecture and award. It means a lot to me and will motivate me to do even more for my people. Zamfara is on the rise.”

Among other dignitaries awarded at the event is the Nasarawa State Governor, Abdullahi A Sule, for his contributions to public service and sustainable development.

World.title: Why I am no fan of couscous, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
My first encounter was aboard an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Washington Dulles to Addis Ababa. I’m still not sure why I chose it. Perhaps I reached for something that looked vaguely familiar. Or perhaps I was momentarily distracted by the flight attendant, a Tigrayan beauty, the sort that once turned a high-profile Nigerian politician to moonlight as a masseur at 35,000 feet. Whatever the reason, I cannot, in good conscience, blame my dislike for it on the taste alone.

As a Nigerian, I understand better than most that food is often an acquired experience. Many of our cherished delicacies would bewilder outsiders. Take ogiri, for instance, a condiment whose distinctive aroma comes from oil bean seeds preserved till rotten at its core. To someone unfamiliar with it, the smell could be pungent. To us, it is culinary gold.

My issue with couscous has always been something else entirely. It looks like Jollof rice but tastes nothing like it. Every spoonful leaves me with the strange feeling that I have been tricked. It resembles, in my admittedly whimsical opinion, a form of culinary deception.

Only later did I learn that couscous is both a staple and a cultural symbol across the Maghreb, especially in Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. Made from tiny granules of semolina that are rolled and steamed into tiny granules, it is far more than just food; it is a shared tradition that binds the region together.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Perhaps it is mere superstition on my part, but I cannot shake the feeling that couscous has become a metaphor for my understanding of North Africa’s complicated relationship with the rest of the continent.

From a distance, North Africa appears unquestionably African. On closer inspection, however, its political orientation, cultural identity and strategic priorities have often looked elsewhere. The continent is acknowledged when convenient, but seldom embraced as a genuine community of equals.

That may sound harsh. It is nevertheless a perception shared by many people south of the Sahara, and it deserves an honest discussion rather than sentimental slogans about African unity.

For most of my life, I have believed deeply in the idea of Africa. Not because we all share the same complexion, language or customs. We clearly do not, but because history placed us within the same geographic destiny. Colonial powers partitioned the continent with little regard for existing civilizations or identities. Whether by accident or design, we inherited a common map. The sensible response is to make the best of that inheritance through solidarity, cooperation and mutual respect. The problem however, is that solidarity cannot be a one-way street.

Increasingly, many sub-Saharan Africans are asking whether North African governments and societies genuinely see themselves as part of the same African project or whether Africa is simply an identity invoked whenever it is politically advantageous.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, there has been widespread and justified outrage over xenophobic violence in South Africa. Africans have repeatedly condemned attacks on foreign nationals and demanded that Pretoria protect migrants regardless of their nationality. The moral principle is sound: Africans should not brutalize fellow Africans simply because they crossed a border in search of opportunity. Yet that same moral outrage seems noticeably muted when similar abuses occur north of the Sahara.

Human rights organisations have documented the mistreatment of migrants from sub-Saharan Africa in several North African countries. Reports have described arbitrary arrests, forced expulsions, racial discrimination and physical abuse, particularly against migrants attempting to reach Europe through Morocco or Libya. The horrifying images that emerged from Libya’s slave markets shocked the world, revealing migrants being bought and sold in what amounted to modern-day slavery. Mauritania continues to struggle with the legacy of hereditary slavery, despite legal prohibitions, with many Haratins still facing severe forms of discrimination and exploitation.

These are not internet rumours. They have been documented by respected international organizations and journalists. None of this means that North African states have no right to enforce their immigration laws. Every sovereign nation has that authority. Nigeria enforces immigration laws. Ghana does. Kenya does. The United States certainly does. The issue is not border enforcement. This is a matter of human dignity.

There is a profound difference between deporting an undocumented migrant and degrading that person’s humanity. The disturbing videos and eyewitness accounts that have emerged over the years are troubling not simply because migrants were arrested, but because many appeared to be treated as though they possessed no intrinsic worth. That should concern every African.

To be fair, responsibility does not rest solely with North African governments.

The greatest tragedy begins much farther south. Corrupt governments across sub-Saharan Africa have systematically destroyed economic opportunity, weakened institutions and stolen the future of their own citizens. Millions of young Africans embark on dangerous migration routes because their leaders have failed them. The Mediterranean has become a cemetery because too many African governments have become indifferent to human suffering.

If Nigeria, Sudan, Eritrea, Mali or other countries provided security, jobs and functioning institutions, far fewer young people would entrust their lives to smugglers. That reality cannot be ignored. Yet acknowledging one injustice does not excuse another.

Another aspect of this conversation concerns identity itself. North African countries understandably possess complex identities shaped by Arab, Amazigh, Mediterranean and African influences. There is nothing inherently wrong with that. Identity is not a zero-sum proposition. The concern arises when African identity becomes largely transactional.

During international sporting competitions, continental organizations and media outlets often celebrate North African victories as triumphs for Africa. African solidarity is loudly proclaimed.

Yet many sub-Saharan Africans wonder whether that solidarity is reciprocated in everyday life, in migration policy, in racial attitudes, in diplomacy and in public discourse. Brotherhood that appears only during football tournaments is not brotherhood. It is branding.

The late Muammar Gaddafi further illustrates the need to distinguish rhetoric from reality. Many admirers portray him as one of Africa’s greatest Pan-Africanists. They point to his advocacy for African unity, his calls for a continental currency and his financial support for the African Union. There is some truth in that narrative. But there is another side.

Gaddafi’s interventions in Liberia, Sierra Leone and elsewhere were hardly exercises in selfless Pan-African idealism. Having being treated like a pariah by countries of the Arab league, he was basically looking for a different sphere of influence and decided where best more than Africa. His government armed and financed rebel movements that prolonged devastating civil wars and cost countless African lives.

Those interventions often served his imperial ambitions far more than the pretext for Africa’s collective interests.

That is not the Pan-Africanism envisioned by Kwame Nkrumah, Nnamdi Azikiwe, Julius Nyerere or Patrice Lumumba. Their vision rested upon liberation, equality and shared development. It did not involve exporting instability to weaker neighbours.

Sub-Saharan Africa must therefore approach its relationship with North Africa with maturity rather than illusion.

Maturity requires neither hostility nor naïveté. North African countries are important economic partners. They possess advanced industries, strategic ports, growing manufacturing sectors and valuable diplomatic influence. Cooperation is beneficial and necessary. But cooperation must rest upon realism.

Sub-Saharan Africa should stop assuming that geography automatically creates solidarity. Relationships between states are ultimately governed by interests. When they diverge, sub-Saharan Africa must defend its own priorities without guilt or apology. Pan-Africanism should not become an excuse for ignoring unequal relationships or remaining silent in the face of discrimination.

African unity cannot survive as a slogan recited at summits while migrants are abused at borders. It cannot flourish if one part of the continent demands solidarity but withholds empathy. Nor can it succeed if sub-Saharan Africans continue to romanticize relationships that are not always reciprocal.

Perhaps that is why I remain unconvinced by couscous. It resembles rice, but it is not rice. Likewise, some relationships resemble brotherhood until circumstances reveal otherwise. The lesson is not that North Africa is the enemy. It is not. The lesson is that genuine partnership must be measured not by speeches, flags or continental geography but by consistent mutual respect.

Sub-Saharan Africa should engage North Africa as equal partners, not imagined siblings bound by sentimental narratives. Friendship should certainly be welcomed wherever it is genuine. Cooperation should be expanded wherever interests converge. But trust, like respect, should be earned rather than assumed.

That is not cynicism. It is simply the beginning of a more honest conversation about what Pan-Africanism ought to mean in the twenty-first century.

And yes, I found myself unable to cheer for either Morocco or Argentina during the just-concluded World Cup. It was my own small act of rebellion against the way both countries have treated folks who look like me.

Osmund Agbo is a medical doctor and author. His works include Black Grit, White Knuckles: The Philosophy of Black Renaissance and the novel The Velvet Court: Courtesan Chronicles. His most recent publications, Pray, Let the Shaman Die and Ma’am, I Do Not Come to You for Love, have just been released.

World.title: Abiodun announces arrest of four more kidnappers of Ogun students, commissions road
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, on Friday commissioned the 3.3-kilometre Adesan Road in Mowe, Obafemi-Owode Local Government Area, as he announced the arrest of four additional suspects linked to the abduction of seven students of Gateway ICT Polytechnic, Saapade.

Governor Abiodun described the rescue of the students and the arrest of the suspects as a major victory in the state’s war against criminality, declaring that Ogun State would never become a safe haven for criminals.

It would be recalled that two members of the kidnapping gang were arrested on Thursday during the operation that led to the successful rescue of the students.

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, the governor expressed appreciation to the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS), the National Association of Ogun State Students (NAOSS), and other student bodies for their patience, understanding, and support throughout the period of the students’ captivity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He attributed the successful rescue operation to the coordinated efforts of security agencies, including the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services (DSS), the Nigerian Army, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), the Ogun State Security Network Agency (Amotekun Corps), local hunters, and vigilantes.

Governor Abiodun also acknowledged the support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Inspector General of Police, and the Director-General of the DSS.

“Sometime before the end of July, some of our students were kidnapped by unscrupulous elements. To the glory of God, with the cooperation and collaboration of our law enforcement agencies and the support we received from Mr. President, the Inspector General of Police and the Director-General of the DSS, we worked night and day.

“Yesterday, we rescued all seven students alive. We have arrested four more of the kidnappers, while the remaining suspects are still on the run. We will arrest them as well,” the governor said.

Reaffirming his administration’s zero tolerance for criminality, Governor Abiodun stressed that Ogun State, as Nigeria’s industrial capital and gateway to the nation, would not permit criminals to operate within its borders.

“Ogun State will not allow crime or criminality. Those who come here to test our resolve will be tracked down, smoked out, arrested, and made to face the full weight of the law,” he declared.

Highlighting his administration’s infrastructure achievements, Governor Abiodun disclosed that 42 roads have been constructed or reconstructed across Ogun Central Senatorial District since 2019, with 12 of them located in Obafemi-Owode Local Government Area. He added that about 1,600 kilometres of roads have been completed across the state’s three senatorial districts.

According to him, roads completed in Obafemi-Owode include the Abeokuta–Sagamu Interchange Road, Panseke–Adigbe Road, Journalists’ Estate Road in Arepo, Siun–Owode Road (Phase I), the revived Mowe–Ofada Road, Iyana-Oloke Junction–MAPOLY Road, Adesan Road, Kuforiji–Olubi Road, Adigbe–Laderin–Train Station Road, Sagamu–Ofada–Papalanto Road, and Magboro–Makogi Road.

“In Ogun Central, within the last seven years, we have reconstructed 42 roads, and we are still constructing more.

“When we assumed office on May 29, 2019, we made several promises. Today, it is gratifying to look back and see how far God has helped us in fulfilling those promises.

“Even as we wind down this administration, we still have more roads to award and complete. There are additional roads in Obafemi-Owode, including the road linking Magboro, that will soon be commissioned. We will remain a promise-keeping administration,” he said.

The governor observed that Obafemi-Owode, being a border local government and the food basket of Ogun State where the renowned Ofada rice is cultivated and processed, deserves sustained investment in infrastructure to support its growing population and expanding economic activities.

He urged residents to protect the newly commissioned road by ensuring its proper use and maintenance.

Earlier, the Commissioner for Works and Infrastructure, Ade Akinsanya, described Adesan Road as a strategic economic corridor that would improve connectivity between adjoining communities and the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, enhance commerce, and ease transportation.

Also speaking, the Chairman of Obafemi-Owode Local Government, Mr Adesina Ogunsola, commended Governor Abiodun for his sustained investment in infrastructure, noting that the road would greatly benefit traders, students, motorists, and other road users.

He disclosed that the local government had complemented the state’s efforts by constructing the 1.6-kilometre Adigbe–Ita-Baale–Idi-Mangoro–Police Post Road and the one-kilometre Ogidan–Gele Odun Road, while additional roads have been earmarked for reconstruction.

The member representing Obafemi-Owode State Constituency in the Ogun State House of Assembly, Hon Damilola Soneye Kayode, thanked the governor for fulfilling a long-standing request for the reconstruction of the road, noting that it serves about six communities and would significantly enhance transportation and economic activities.

Also, the member representing Obafemi-Owode, Odeda and Abeokuta North Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives, Hon Olumide Osoba, applauded the governor for delivering yet another strategic infrastructure project, describing it as a reflection of the administration’s commitment to inclusive development.

In his remarks, the Olu of Mowe, Oba Oriyomi Yahaya, commended Governor Abiodun for fulfilling his campaign promise to the people of Mowe and appealed to him to also reconstruct the town’s market to further stimulate commerce and economic growth.

World.title: Infantile Infantino should exit for trying to sell the World Cup, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
In reality, the Infantino gang tried to commercialise the soul of football, a unifying force of humanity. He had dangled a $40 million award to every association that voted for his plans, promising that an advance $30 million would be made available to each of the federations by 1 January, 2027.

Gianni Infantino, the Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) President who stole into office a decade ago on the back of a coup against Sepp Blatter, may be on his way out. He has become like an orphan caught with his hand in the till.

The 2026 World Cup was quite successful. It was also a commercial success, with FIFA raking in a record revenue of $13 billion to $15 billion. The World Cup, which had thirteen teams at inception, has expanded to a record 48 teams and a total of 104 matches. This has led to high-volume ticket sales. Broadcasting rights alone in 2026 generated about $4.2 billion. Sponsorship and hospitality added to the income.

Admittedly, FIFA’s costs also went up. For instance, a higher $871 million was allocated to the teams, including a $655 million base prize. The champions, Spain, took $51 million; runners-up, $34 million; and third place, $30 million. Also, holding the competition in three venues – the United States, Mexico and Canada – increased the logistical overhead. But, overall, it was a hugely successful tournament.

However, as the world celebrated and discussed the games, the Infantino leadership decided to take advantage of the euphoria by sneaking in a partial privatisation package.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

As it turned out, without consultations with the regional bodies, the leadership created a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise, with which it was going to sell a 20-30 per cent stake in World Cup commercial rights to private investors led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared. Infantino said the plan was to raise a minimum of $20 billion.

In reality, the Infantino gang tried to commercialise the soul of football, a unifying force of humanity. He had dangled a $40 million award to every association that voted for his plans, promising that an advance $30 million would be made available to each of the federations by 1 January, 2027.

However, an immediate rejection came from the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), the umbrella body of 55 members of FIFA’s total 211. The region also runs the world’s most lucrative league.

The UEFA knockout punch was its decision to boycott FIFA if the Infantino team went ahead with its greedy plans. The implication of such a boycott is that FIFA may be split and Europe can hold a parallel World Cup with teams that ally with it. The North American confederation, CONCACAF, also joined UEFA in rejecting the FIFA plan.

UEFA declared the attempted privatisation of the World Cup unacceptable and a line that football’s governing institutions must not cross. It added that: “UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.”

To underscore the seriousness with which it is handling the matter, UEFA sent FIFA a preservation letter. It demanded that the world body preserve all evidence, as this may turn out to be a lawsuit.

The UEFA knockout punch was its decision to boycott FIFA if the Infantino team went ahead with its greedy plans. The implication of such a boycott is that FIFA may be split and Europe can hold a parallel World Cup with teams that ally with it. The North American confederation, CONCACAF, also joined UEFA in rejecting the FIFA plan.

Equally, the Asian Football Confederation, AFC, declared it stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF, describing the FIFA leader’s actions as “totally unacceptable.”

However, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) did not take a concrete position on the matter, preferring to keep the door open, which is an indirect endorsement of the plan.

However, things began to crumble around Infantino. Some officials of FIFA distanced themselves from the plan. FIFA’s head of global football development and famous coach, Arsene Wenger, said he was “not aware” of the Infantino gambit.

In conceding defeat, Infantino and FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström issued a joint statement after a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, stating that: “We acknowledge mistakes were made in the process of the proposed establishment of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). It was certainly not the intention for the FIFA Council and FIFA Member Associations to feel excluded from the process and it should have been handled differently.” They followed with a clarification and a warning: “Furthermore, as already known, the proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the FIFA Member Associations and the FIFA Council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, FIFA will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.”

Another alternative way to replace Infantino is to wait until the 77th FIFA Congress scheduled to be held in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March, 2027, where he can be voted out. FIFA was established on 21 May, 1904, and the first World Cup was held in 1930, with Uruguay defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final to win the maiden edition. As it stands, Infantino is a danger to world football.

But the warning appeared to have had little effect. UEFA, looking beyond the FIFA statement, declared that although Infantino has beaten a retreat, this “must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.”

It implied that Infantino must fall. Equally, the AFC, looking beyond the Infantino backdown, demanded that FIFA’s future actions must be “shaped through proper consultation.” This is an indication that a post-Infantino FIFA era should commence. What the Infantino team tried to carry out was like a coup, and there are implications for a failed coup.

The options for Infantino’s welcome replacement include impeaching him. This will require a minimum of 41 member associations calling for an extraordinary congress, where an impeachment motion would need a simple majority to pass.

A second alternative is for his case to be tabled at the FIFA Independent Ethics Committee, which is empowered to remove a FIFA president, as was done to the immediate past president, Sepp Blatter.

Another issue of ethics that Infantino faces is taking dictation from United States President Donald Trump, who personally called him to have the red card issued to USA striker, Folarin Balogun, at the 2026 World Cup be overturned. Balogun was expected to miss the last-16 clash against Belgium after picking up a red card for an unsportsmanlike challenge of Bosnia’s Tarik Muharemovi. FIFA, in compliance with Trump’s political directive, suspended the ban, clearing Balogun to play against Belgium. The latter beat the USA 4-1 in the 6 July match.

Infantino had also been accused of removing two chairmen and all but two members of the Ethics Committee, which implied that he did not want the body to investigate corruption against the FIFA governing body. He was also accused of influencing the candidature of Ahmad Ahmad as CAF president.

Another alternative way to replace Infantino is to wait until the 77th FIFA Congress scheduled to be held in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March, 2027, where he can be voted out. FIFA was established on 21 May, 1904, and the first World Cup was held in 1930, with Uruguay defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final to win the maiden edition. As it stands, Infantino is a danger to world football.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: An appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and all Nigerians: Stop the NFF elections, please! By Segun Odegbami
World.content:
Odegbami

On March 22, 1998, I was officially decorated with the honour and title of ‘Sports Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Nigeria’ in Abuja by the then Minister of Sports. It was in addition to a previous national honour of ‘Member of the Order of the Niger’, MON.

I take both honours very seriously. They are earned, the rewards for national duty through hard work, dedication, sacrifices, patriotism, discipline, and trophies.

They also come, of course, with additional demands and even more responsibility.

That’s why I try, always, to appreciate the country’s generosity by attempting to live a simple, decent life of exemplary good conduct to serve as a model for generations coming after me through the window of sports. How far I have fared with these unwritten expectations and standards I leave for Nigerians and posterity to judge.

Today, football in Nigeria is at a crossroads. The time comes to test my judgement and character, a burden that I must carry even in the evening of my life.

I find that there is really nothing for me to lose in standing by what I believe are the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth! To be silent now means to fail the government, the people and the game of football itself. So, I am raising my voice again.

Nigerians know me for my activities and contributions in sports and in football, in particular – playing the game, administering it, organising it, promoting it, deploying it as a tool to drive education, empowerment, health, patriotism, eradication of illiteracy, diplomacy and national orientation.

It all started in 1973. As an undergraduate student I was invited to the national football team of Nigeria, the Green Eagles, from the National Sports Festival, to start a relationship that has remained unbroken to this day.

In the 53 years since then, I played for the country; rose to be Captain of the national team and also of the national contingent to the Olympic Games; administered the game as a member of the board of the Nigerian Football Association and as Chairman of the Governing Council of the National Institute of Sports; single-handedly managed two Nigerian athletes (in a sport outside of football) to win Gold and Silver medals at the Olympic Games; served in several panels, commissions and committees promoting sports and seeking solutions to challenges in Nigerian sports; established an NGO/institution that has been promoting the combination of sports and scholarship; facilitating the migration of Nigerian student/athletes to Colleges and Universities in the USA and in India; and currently serving as head of a new and special unit developing a template and policies for sports diplomacy within Nigeria’s foreign affairs.

The measure of my work in all these national assignments are an open book for all Nigerians to see and determine.

All those experiences count in the position I have now chosen to take in the unfortunate present situation the country finds itself. With all the talented footballers that the country parades all over the world, it is a sad commentary that at international level, achievements have reached a plateau, and even started to decline. This is easily measured in the successes, or lack of them, that the country’s football has achieved in recent times. Some of the results are totally unacceptable, needless to mention them here.

The reality is that football administration in the past two decades, in particular, has not matched or complimented the level of talent and possible achievements.

The growth of our football industry has been stunted by faulty decisions taken more in ignorance than by any malicious intentions since the early part of the 1990s. These have grown, sustained and become the norm in our football, a monster that now needs the creators of it to rid it of its venom. They won’t do it because they are also the beneficiaries of the faulty architecture!

Next month, an election into the board of the Nigerian Football Association will take place. I am deliberately using the word ‘association’ because that is the starting point of all the anomalies in the present administrative architecture. This takes careful understanding that I cannot explain here , but that will make sense when the matter is tabled before a civil court for interrogation, and where a subsisting judgment to amend it has been treated with levity for almost 8 years. In law, the Nigerian Football Federation does not even exist!

As for the elections the way things are now, they have been held and sewn up already, the results determined even before a vote has been cast. The persons that can contest and will, know themselves already. Those to be deprived of the opportunity to even contest have been isolated and sent on a wild goose chase, to go around Nigeria furtively searching for endorsements they will not get in a rushed and harried election. The winners of elections have already been determined by the same group of people in office now.

The elections will also be conducted away from any prying eyes to avoid any chances of transparency, and where bribery and corrupt practices can be conducted without consequence, far from the headquarters of the federation and the supervising National Sports Commission that would have ensured neutrality.

The issues are long and endless that need the supervising ministry’s intervention. The NSC cannot do anything with their hands tied by ‘fictitious’ threats by ‘FIFA’ that have no substance in any statutes anywhere in the world.

In short, history, documents, facts and figures are essential ingredients that will illuminate the clouded areas of our football structures in order for the ship of our football to be steadied for future development.

My experiences cannot be bought in the market place or discountenanced. My current works speak for themselves. My suggestions for the future should at least be given some attention.

Therefore, I am writing this publicly with some concern but a deep sense of responsibility and sincerity. Elections into the board of the NFF have become a four-yearly ritual of crisis. The process used in conducting them have always been contentious, and were always challenged as a result of perceived irregularities and manipulation.

All of these to the detriment of the country that loves its football with passion but can only look on helplessly as football continues to suffer and fails to achieve its full potentials, fails to boost the country’s economy, and fails to empower the country’s gifted youths with the best opportunities that are available all over the world.

In the next few days, I shall be taking documents that are currently used in the administration of Nigerian football to the Nigerian civil courts for interrogation and interpretation, to explain to Nigerians documented facts about the real power and roles of FIFA in our country’s internal football affairs; the status, interpretation, role and place of State Football Associations; the equity in unequal and lopsided representation by members; the place and role of government as the biggest funder of football in the country; the justification for the convoluted, politicized, expensive conduct of ordinary football elections in Nigeria, and so on!

The next few weeks will be very interesting.

I hope all Nigerians, including the members of the Nigerian Football Association will understand why these elections should be temporarily halted for Nigerian football to find its feet again!

Olusegun Odegbami, MON, OLY, MON, AFNIIA, FNIS

Sports Ambassador, Federal Republic of Nigeria; Grand Sports Ambassador of Ogun State.

World.title: Out from prison, Nigeria’s Daga bounces back
World.content:
Daga

.Scores 2 goals in 2 games after acquittal for rape

By Douglas Baye-Osagie

Three years ago, Daniel Daga was Nigeria’s next big thing. A defensive midfielder in the Sunday Oliseh mould — strong, intelligent, with delicate long-range passing and an eye for goal. At 17 he was an Enyimba Football Club mainstay, playing for Nigeria’s most successful club. He then played for the Flying Eagles at back-to-back U20 FIFA World Cups in 2023 and 2025. At 18 he made the move every Nigerian boy dreams of — Europe — signing for Norway’s Molde FK. Where talent becomes stardom. Or dies trying.

Suddenly, a few months after arriving in Europe, news of a rape allegation hit the internet. “This can’t be true,” some of us screamed.

In December 2025, Molde removed him from training and matchday activities after he was formally charged over an alleged sexual offence involving an unnamed woman. The case reportedly dated back to April 2025. It echoed what happened to another young Nigerian, Akinkunmi Amoo, who was accused and later convicted of rape in Denmark while playing for FC Copenhagen. Everyone following Daga’s career prayed for justice — we did not want to see a bright future derailed.

In March 2026, a Norwegian district court convicted Daga and sentenced him to six months in prison for a sexual act without consent. Daga maintained his innocence, with his lawyer arguing the encounter was consensual, and an appeal was filed. Molde kept him out of the squad while the legal process continued.

The case took a decisive turn in July. Norway’s Frostating Court of Appeal unanimously acquitted Daga, overturning the earlier conviction. Molde subsequently confirmed that the midfielder was again available for selection. From suspension to a fresh start.

Daga’s return has been emphatic. He marked his comeback against KFUM with an emotional goal, then scored again against Sarpsborg — a powerful reminder of his ability after an extremely challenging period. The focus is now back where he wants it: on the pitch.

When news first filtered out of Norway, the reaction back home was instant and brutal. Social media buried him. Pundits wrote him off. For a boy who was the face of Enyimba at 16, it felt like the dream was over before it truly began.

Daga was not just another export. He was the NPFL’s proof that local football could still produce world-class midfielders. Composed, strong, and tactically smart beyond his years, he captained the Flying Eagles and bossed games for Enyimba as a teenager. Europe came calling because he looked ready.

Then came the case. The details were messy, the headlines were louder, and the process was slow. Whether guilty or not, the stain stuck. Contracts were paused. Confidence dipped. For months, the player who once played like he had nothing to lose looked like a boy who had everything to lose.

But here is the truth we rarely say in football: a man does not fall forever. Sometimes the fall is what teaches you how to stand properly. Daga is out of that process now and learning to pick his steps again. That is why people are talking about a “second coming.” His return to the pitch is the best thing that happened to Nigerian football in the month of July.

To understand why this matters and gives me so much joy you have to look back. Nigerian football has seen this movie before. Talent derailed not by injury, but by off-field trouble. The first name that comes to mind is Etim Esin.

Etim “Maradona” Esin was arguably the most gifted Nigerian midfielder of the late 80s and 90s. At 18 he was in the Flying Eagles, Olympic team and Super Eagles. He was the darling of the local league before he was scouted to Belgium, with technique that made defenders look foolish. Everyone said he would be our greatest ever.

Before we could blink, he was arrested and charged in connection with a rape case involving a minor. He spent time in detention before being released. Legally, the case ended. Professionally, it never did. While he was away trying to sort himself out, Friday Ekpo and then Jay Okocha emerged.

From national team regular to forgotten man in less than two years. By the time Okocha made his Super Eagles home debut against Algeria in 1993, the fans had forgotten about Etim Esin completely. Esin later spoke about depression, financial ruin, and how one incident cut a career that should have lasted 20 years down to less than 10. He remains a cautionary tale in every Nigerian dressing room.

Rape accusations can be career-threatening and make life unbearable for a footballer. Remember the recent cases of Benjamin Mendy, the French World Cup winner, and Thomas Partey of Ghana. In July 2025, the Arsenal and Black Stars midfielder was charged with multiple counts of rape relating to alleged incidents between 2021 and 2022. He pleaded not guilty.

The impact was immediate. Arsenal let his contract run down. Sponsors went quiet. Ghana fans were split. He was even denied entry to Canada during the World Cup and missed Ghana’s first game in Toronto. Whether he is eventually cleared or convicted, Partey has already lost momentum at 32 — an age where every season counts for a midfielder.

That is the cruel part. It is not easy to maintain focus when rape charges land. The mind is not on the ball. It’s on survival, rebuilding lost relationships, and trying to hold your concentration together.

That is why the return to the pitch of Daniel Daga case feels so important. He is 20. He is not at the end. He is at the beginning. We are all happy he has been set free because his talent is what we need going forward for the Olympics team in 2028 and possibly the World Cup in 2030. If he gets this right, the Norway episode becomes a footnote. If he gets it wrong, it becomes his entire Wikipedia page.

The problem is cultural too. Young African players go to Europe with talent but without structure. No media training. No understanding that in Europe, your name is your brand, and one mistake travels around the world in 10 minutes.

For Daga, the path back is simple but hard. Good he has played 3 league games and scored in two since his return back to the pitch in July. The same work rate that made him stand out in Aba is going to help him succeed .The same humility that let a teenager lead senior men at Enyimba. Talent got him to Europe. Character will keep him there. Mendy is trying to rebuild. Partey is fighting his case. Esin never fully recovered. Daga still has time and with focus he will get to the very top.

From Cristiano Ronaldo to Celestine Babayaro to Quinton Fortune to Rio Ferdinand — superstars who faced rape allegations and fought to rebuild their careers.

So here is to the second coming of Daniel Daga. May he remember that a fall is not a finish line. And may Daga prove that a Nigerian boy can stumble in Europe, stand up, and still become the midfielder we all saw coming. The pitch is waiting.

World.title: Imo monarch’s murder: 5 suspects arrested, gang kingpin killed in shootout
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The Force headquarters disclosed on Saturday that Police operatives have recorded a breakthrough in the ongoing investigation into the murder of HRH Eze Paulinus Ekwueme, Ochia I of Ochia Kingdom, and five others in Ohaji/Egbema, Imo State.

Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Aniete Iniedu, made the disclosure, noting that two other suspects were killed during exchange of fire between the gang and policemen.

He said, “Following actionable intelligence, operatives of the Special Tactics Squad, Force Intelligence Department (STS-FID), conducted a series of operations between 2nd and 6th August, 2026, targeting members of the criminal syndicate allegedly linked to the incident.

“The operations culminated in the early hours of 6th August, 2026, when operatives located the hideout of a suspected gang kingpin, identified as Ojiogu Elumah Martin, alias ‘Acid’, in Ohaji/Egbema.

“The suspect engaged the operatives in a gun duel and sustained injuries during the encounter, which subsequently led to his death. One AK-47 rifle, three magazines and 56 rounds of 7.62mm live ammunition were recovered from the scene.

“The suspect was identified as an alleged leader of the criminal syndicate linked to the attack of 10th April, 2026, in which the monarch and five others were killed along the Asa/Awara Road, Ohaji/Egbema, while returning to Owerri.

“Four suspects had earlier been arrested in connection with the incident, while two others reportedly died during previous encounters with the Police.

“Following the latest operation, efforts have been intensified to apprehend other fleeing members of the syndicate, establish the full extent of their involvement and recover further operational intelligence and exhibits.

“The Nigeria Police Force remains committed to ensuring that all persons found to be connected with the crime are brought to justice and that every effort is made to bring the investigation to a logical conclusion.”

World.title: History Made, Future Beckons: How Oloyede’s stewardship redefined JAMB, restored public trust
World.content:
JAMB Registrar Prof Ishaq Oloyede

By Ishola Balogun

After ten eventful years at the helm of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board

(JAMB), Professor Is-haq Olanrewaju Oloyede on Friday formally handed over the

leadership of Nigeria’s foremost admissions agency to Professor Segun Aina, bringing to a close a tenure widely associated with sweeping institutional reforms, technological innovation, financial transparency and renewed public confidence in the nation’s tertiary admissions process.

Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker

Speaking at the handover ceremony held at JAMB’s National Headquarters in Bwari, Abuja, Prof. Oloyede described the occasion as both a moment of gratitude and reflection, declaring that whatever achievements were recorded during his stewardship were products of divine grace and collective effort rather than personal accomplishment.

“It is with a profound sense of gratitude to the Almighty Allah and immense appreciation to all people of goodwill that I address this distinguished audience today,” he said.

“I return all glory to Almighty Allah, whose boundless mercy, wisdom and grace sustained me throughout these remarkable ten years. Through periods of daunting challenges, difficult policy decisions and far-reaching institutional reforms, His guidance remained my greatest source of strength. Whatever accomplishments have been recorded during this period are not mine alone; they are manifestations of His infinite favour and blessings.”

The outgoing Registrar recalled that when he assumed office on August 9, 2016, he deliberately chose the theme, “Let’s Do It Together,” believing that no institution could succeed without collaboration.

“I had no illusion right from the outset that I would depend on God’s guidance and people’s support,” he said. “Doing it together means that many colours make a rainbow and many flowers make a garden.”

A decade built on five pillars

Reflecting on his stewardship, Prof. Oloyede said his administration was anchored on five cardinal principles—staff welfare, discipline, technology, transparency and networking—which became the foundation of JAMB’s transformation.

“When I took over the mandate of leadership at JAMB, I outlined five cardinal points that my administration would be anchored on… In these five, though perfection belongs to the Almighty Allah, I can confidently say we tried our best.”

Welfare before productivity

He explained that his administration invested heavily in staff welfare, arguing that no institution could outperform the people who run it.

Among the initiatives introduced were timely promotions, improved work environments, rehabilitation and construction of offices nationwide, over N8 billion contributed to staff retirement savings, retirement benefits ranging between N3 million and N10 million, the introduction of a 13th-month salary, examination duty allowances increased from 10 to 20 per cent, free daily meals, transport support for key operational staff and medical interventions, including N12 million approved for the treatment of a staff member at the National Hospital.

Exceptional staff were rewarded with cash prizes and awards, while one zonal office and a Professional Test Centre complex were named after a deserving employee.

“We stood by our decision because without dedicated and motivated staff, we won’t achieve the JAMB that Nigeria deserves,” he declared.

Beyond staff welfare, he said candidates also benefited from reforms, including a 30 per cent reduction in the UTME application cost and comprehensive support for candidates with special needs through sponsorship, accommodation, feeding and refund of application fees.

The Board also extended institutional support through the National Tertiary Admissions Performance Merit (NATAPM) Award, disbursing approximately ¦ 750 million annually to tertiary institutions.

Discipline without compromise

While investing in welfare, Oloyede maintained that discipline remained non-negotiable.

“It is said that the first law in heaven is discipline and indiscipline is the mother of all evils.”

According to him, more than ten staff members faced prosecution over allegations of misconduct during his tenure.

He recalled the widely publicised case involving the infamous claim that a snake swallowed ¦ 36 million, describing it as one of the disciplinary measures undertaken to restore accountability.

“The sensationalised case of a snake gulping N36 million that the media feasted on was just one of the measures taken to entrench discipline,” he said, recalling that even the EFCC had remarked at the time that “an eagle shows no mercy for money-swallowing snakes.”

He added that the insistence on discipline accounted for JAMB’s consistent remittance of billions of naira in operational surpluses to the Federal Government.

Technology as the engine of reform

Perhaps the defining feature of his administration, Oloyede noted, was JAMB’s aggressive deployment of technology.

He listed the expansion of Computer-Based Testing (CBT), development of the Central Admissions Processing System (CAPS), biometric identity verification, CCTV surveillance, digital PINs and payment platforms, Remote Authoring and Moderation System (RAMS), digital institutional reforms and the Bring-Your-Device initiative as milestones achieved during the decade.

“At the heart of our operational blueprint is technology and we owe many of our far-reaching reforms to innovative technologies,” he said.

Reflecting on recent technical challenges experienced during the UTME, Oloyede admitted that no technology is infallible.

“What happened last year which made me emotional was proof that technology has its limits, just like everything human, and eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.”

Transparency restores confidence

On transparency, the outgoing Registrar said his administration deliberately opened JAMB’s operations to public scrutiny.

“Our operational and financial transactions are in the open domain and our weekly newsletter always contains details of our activities and finances.”

He described CAPS as one of the Board’s most revolutionary innovations.

“With a system like CAPS, admissions into our institutions are transparent and anyone can question why a candidate is not admitted despite meriting it.”

According to him, the notorious culture of secret or “under-the-table” admissions has largely become a thing of the past.

“My belief is that transparency transforms institutions by eliminating toxic silos.”

Partnerships That Strengthened the Institution

Prof. Oloyede credited much of JAMB’s success to strategic partnerships with government agencies, tertiary institutions, security organisations, examination bodies, the media and over 1,010 private CBT centre owners.

“We could not have achieved anything without leveraging networks and partnerships.”

He acknowledged the cooperation of the National Security Adviser, the Director-General of the Department of State Services, the National Intelligence Agency, the Nigeria Police Force, NSCDC, EFCC, ICPC, NIMC, NCC, Vice Chancellors, Rectors, Provosts, civil society organisations and professional associations within and outside Nigeria.

He also highlighted the establishment of the Nigerian Educational Assessment Academy (NEAA), created alongside 18 national agencies to train educational assessment professionals.

“TEAM means Together Everyone Achieves More,” he said. “That became our mantra.”

Gratitude to leaders, stakeholders

Throughout his address, Oloyede repeatedly acknowledged those he said made JAMB’s transformation possible.

He expressed gratitude to former President Muhammadu Buhari for appointing him, former President Olusegun Obasanjo for earlier identifying his leadership potential, and President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for retaining confidence in him.

He also thanked Minister of Education Dr. Maruf Tunji Alausa, former Minister Prof. Tahir Mamman, Minister of State for Education Prof. Suwaiba Said Ahmad, Permanent Secretary Abel Enitan and former Permanent Secretary Sonny Echono.

Several governors also received special recognition for donating land, office complexes, vehicles and Professional Test Centres across the country.

Among those acknowledged were Prof. Babagana Zulum of Borno State, whose government built and donated the North-East Mega Professional Test Centre and named it after him; Nyesom Wike for providing office facilities and land in Rivers State within 24 hours of his request; Babatunde Raji Fashola for facilitating Certificates of Occupancy for JAMB properties; Ibikunle Amosun and Dapo Abiodun for supporting the South-West Mega Professional Test Centre project; Godwin Obaseki for relocating JAMB’s Edo office to a befitting site; Rochas Okorocha for land allocation in Imo State; Babajide Sanwo-Olu for allocating lands across Lagos State; AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq and Douye Diri for assisting JAMB’s facilities in Kwara and Bayelsa States.

He also appreciated private individuals including Ahmad Raji (SAN) for donating a fully equipped Professional Test Centre in Iseyin and Dr. Wale Babalakin for repeatedly making the Bola Babalakin Hall available free of charge for JAMB’s annual policy meetings.

The outgoing Registrar equally paid tribute to past Registrars, Governing Board members, directors, staff unions, retired employees, examination bodies, tertiary institutions, civil society groups, candidates, parents, security agencies, professional organisations and members of the media.

“I seldom say it in order to keep you on your toes,” he told JAMB staff. “But I now say it loud: thank you very much.”

A legacy beyond infrastructure

Oloyede noted that beyond physical infrastructure, JAMB under his watch earned national and international recognition for accountability, technological innovation and service delivery.

He disclosed that Prof. Emeritus Peter Okebukola had documented about 200 achievements recorded during the administration, while acknowledging the contributions of numerous academics and professionals who helped shape the Board’s reforms.

“The story of JAMB is that of continuous progress,” he said, insisting that his administration merely built upon foundations laid by previous Registrars.

Passing the baton

Turning to his successor, Prof. Segun Aina, Oloyede expressed confidence that the Board’s future remains secure.

“As I hand over the leadership of this great institution, I do so with absolute confidence in its future.”

He described Aina as a younger ICT expert capable of taking JAMB to greater heights.

“I wish my successor great success and his success is the success of all of us who have been privileged to steer JAMB since its inception.”

“My belief is that the advantage and vibrancy of his younger age and his ICT expertise would propel the Board to higher heights than previously attained.”

He pledged to remain available whenever his advice might be needed while urging Nigerians to support the new Registrar.

“There is no success without a successor. They should rather support and pray for Prof. Aina’s success. It is time to face the future with renewed vigour.”

A Personal Farewell

As he prepared to leave office, the former Registrar became reflective, thanking his wife, children, grandchildren and close friends for standing by him throughout what he described as a demanding national assignment.

“It is now over,” he said quietly.

He concluded by once again committing JAMB’s future to God.

“Finally, I thank Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving Nigeria through this noble institution. May He continue to guide, protect and bless the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board in the faithful discharge of its statutory responsibilities for generations to come.”

With those words, Nigerians have witnessed one of the most consequential tenures in the history of JAMB—a decade marked by ambitious reforms, uncompromising accountability, digital transformation and an enduring insistence that institutional success is achieved not by one individual, but by collective purpose.

World.title: 10 phones with the quality cameras in 2026, excluding iPhones
World.content:
Smartphone cameras have become remarkably powerful, with manufacturers increasingly competing on sensor size, megapixel counts, optical zoom and computational photography.

While Apple’s iPhones remain popular among mobile photographers, several Android manufacturers now offer phones with camera systems capable of capturing exceptional levels of detail.

From Samsung and Xiaomi to OPPO, vivo and Honor, here are 10 phones with some of the sharpest cameras available in 2026.

1. OPPO Find X9 Ultra

The OPPO Find X9 Ultra sits firmly among the most ambitious camera phones available.

Its camera system is designed for photographers who want detail across different shooting situations, from standard photographs to distant subjects.

Its combination of advanced sensors, powerful image processing and high-quality zoom makes it particularly attractive to users who want a phone capable of producing highly detailed images without relying on additional camera equipment.

2. Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra

Samsung’s Ultra series has become synonymous with versatile smartphone photography, and the Galaxy S26 Ultra continues that approach.

Its camera setup gives users several focal-length options, making it suitable for everything from everyday photography to portraits and long-distance shots.

The phone is particularly impressive when it comes to zoom photography, allowing users to capture distant subjects while retaining a high level of detail.

3. Xiaomi 17 Ultra

The Xiaomi 17 Ultra is another serious contender for photographers who prioritise image quality.

Its large main camera sensor is designed to capture plenty of light and detail, while its telephoto system gives users greater flexibility when photographing distant subjects.

For anyone looking for a flagship Android phone with an emphasis on photography, the Xiaomi 17 Ultra deserves consideration.

4. vivo X300 Pro

vivo has increasingly positioned its flagship smartphones as camera-focused devices, and the X300 Pro is one of its strongest examples.

The phone is particularly well suited to portrait and telephoto photography.

Its camera processing helps preserve detail while producing images with strong colours and clarity, making it a compelling option for mobile photographers.

5. OPPO Find X9 Pro

The OPPO Find X9 Pro combines flagship-level hardware with a camera system designed for detailed photographs.

It is capable of producing sharp images in a variety of conditions, while its portrait and zoom capabilities add versatility.

The device is especially appealing to users who want a premium camera experience alongside fast performance and modern Android features.

6. Huawei Pura 90s Pro Max

Huawei’s Pura series has developed a reputation for putting photography at the centre of its flagship smartphones.

The Pura 90s Pro Max follows that tradition with sophisticated camera hardware and a strong focus on zoom photography.

Its high-resolution telephoto camera is particularly useful for capturing distant subjects with plenty of detail.

7. Honor Magic 8 Pro

The Honor Magic 8 Pro is another Android flagship worth considering for photography.

The phone’s camera system performs particularly well in challenging lighting conditions, where maintaining detail can be difficult for smartphone cameras.

It also offers a versatile setup for users who want to shoot portraits, landscapes and distant subjects.

8. Xiaomi 17

Not everyone wants a huge smartphone, and the Xiaomi 17 offers a more compact option without abandoning flagship photography.

Its camera system is capable of producing detailed photographs while maintaining a smaller overall footprint.

For buyers who want a high-end camera phone that is easier to handle, the Xiaomi 17 is an interesting alternative.

9. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

Foldable phones have traditionally lagged behind conventional flagships in camera hardware, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra takes a more ambitious approach.

The device combines the large foldable display with a high-end camera system, making it useful for people who want both productivity and photography capabilities in one device.

Its large screen can also make editing and reviewing photographs more convenient.

10. Xiaomi 15 Ultra

Despite being an older model than some of the phones on this list, the Xiaomi 15 Ultra remains a formidable camera phone.

Its large main sensor and high-resolution periscope telephoto camera give it excellent versatility, particularly for users who enjoy photographing distant subjects.

It remains a strong choice for anyone who wants flagship-level smartphone photography without necessarily buying the newest model.
